protocols.clinicalDefinitionEn: Back pain assessment decomposed from NHS.UK's published when-to-get-help guidance. Adult patient. Female.

initialAssessmentQuestions.promptTextEn: What is the person's exact age and sex, are they pregnant/recently postpartum, and where is the pain? Include trauma, cancer/immunocompromise, fever, anticoagulants, urinary symptoms, safeguarding concerns, and whether pain spreads to the chest, abdomen, or legs.
When did the pain start, and did it follow an injury or accident?
Any numbness, tingling, or weakness in either leg?

questions.questionTextEn: Is there numbness, tingling or weakness in BOTH legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or back passage, new difficulty controlling bladder or bowel, chest pain, or did the pain start after a serious accident such as a car crash or a fall from height?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK back pain guidance lists bilateral leg symptoms, saddle numbness, new bladder/bowel changes, sexual dysfunction, concurrent chest pain, and a major-trauma trigger as its own emergency ambulance or Emergency Department criteria - possible cauda equina syndrome or major trauma.

questions.questionTextEn: Does the caller feel hot, cold, shivery, or generally unwell, OR is this severe pain that started suddenly and is quickly getting worse?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance flags fever/feeling unwell with back pain, and sudden severe or rapidly worsening pain, as needing a same-day primary-care review or urgent clinical review call.

questions.questionTextEn: Has the pain lasted several weeks despite home treatment, is it interfering with daily activities, is there unexplained weight loss, a new lump or change in the shape of the back, is it worse at night or with rest, worse with coughing or straining, or is it upper back pain between the shoulder blades?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance lists these as reasons to book a routine primary-care review rather than manage entirely at home.

questions.questionTextEn: Is this mild-to-moderate pain of gradual onset with none of the concerning features above?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance recommends staying active, anti-inflammatory medicine, and heat/ice for uncomplicated back pain without red-flag features.

careAdvice.instructionTextEn: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive for new bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness, progressive leg weakness, major trauma, collapse, or severe systemic illness. Keep the person still and do not make them stand or walk when spinal compromise is possible. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow 999 CPR instructions. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care. Call Back If: worsening leg weakness; new saddle numbness or bladder/bowel change; reduced consciousness or abnormal breathing.
Arrange same-day or next-day medical review. Rest in a comfortable position and avoid heavy lifting until seen. Call Back If: numbness spreads; fever worsens.

Book a routine primary-care appointment through the approved Qatar pathway. Continue gentle activity and use only governance-approved pain relief in the meantime. Call Back If: pain suddenly worsens; new leg numbness or weakness.

careAdvice.instructionTextEn: For an adult only, use gentle activity as tolerated and avoid prolonged bed rest or provoking strain. Wrapped cool or warm packs may be used without direct skin exposure. Medicine choice/dose requires age, weight, pregnancy, allergy, kidney/liver disease, ulcer/bleeding risk, anticoagulants, and current medicines under the approved Qatar pathway. Call Back If: pain does not improve; new numbness, weakness, fever, trauma, or bladder/bowel changes.

Keep the person still and do not make them stand or walk when spinal compromise is possible. If unresponsive and not breathing normally, follow 999 CPR instructions. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.

initialAssessmentQuestions.promptTextEn: What is the person's exact age and sex, are they pregnant, anticoagulated, or known to have a bleeding disorder, how long/severely has bleeding continued despite uninterrupted pressure, and was there trauma, surgery, foreign body, or safeguarding concern?
Did the bleeding start after a blow to the head?
Is the caller taking blood-thinning medication such as warfarin?

questions.questionTextEn: Is there difficulty breathing, reduced consciousness, collapse, faintness or shock, major facial/head trauma, or severe uncontrolled bleeding that is rapidly worsening?
questions.rationaleEn: Immediate life-threatening features require Qatar 999. This separates ambulance need from other NHS.UK Emergency Department criteria that may be stable enough for governed non-ambulance transport.

questions.questionTextEn: After uninterrupted pinching of the soft nose, has bleeding continued longer than 10-15 minutes, does it still seem excessive, is the person swallowing a lot of blood and vomiting, or did it begin after a blow to the head without the immediate life-threatening features above?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK directs these features to Emergency Department and says not to self-drive, while allowing either another driver or an ambulance. Exact Qatar destination and transport choice remain local approval required.

questions.questionTextEn: Is the patient a child under 2, does the caller have regular nosebleeds, anaemia symptoms, take blood-thinning medication, or have a clotting disorder such as haemophilia?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance recommends a primary-care review for these situations even when the bleed itself has stopped.

questions.questionTextEn: Is this a single, brief nosebleed with none of the features above?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance describes standard first aid as sufficient for an uncomplicated nosebleed.

careAdvice.instructionTextEn: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive for severe/uncontrolled bleeding, breathing compromise, faintness/shock, major facial/head trauma, or reduced consciousness. Sit forward if alert, spit blood out, and pinch the soft nose continuously. Do not tilt the head back, lie flat, pack the nose deeply, or repeatedly release pressure to check. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care. Call Back If: bleeding remains uncontrolled; difficulty breathing, swallowing large amounts of blood, faintness, or shock; major trauma or reduced consciousness.

Continue sitting forward and pinching the soft nose while arranging prompt in-person emergency assessment through the Qatar governance-approved pathway. Do not self-drive. A safe adult may transport a stable patient only if the approved local pathway permits; call 999 for breathing difficulty, reduced consciousness, collapse, shock, major trauma, or rapidly worsening/uncontrolled bleeding. Exact destination and transport remain local approval required. Call Back If: difficulty breathing, faintness, collapse, or reduced consciousness; bleeding becomes rapidly worse or remains uncontrolled; major trauma.
Arrange primary-care review through the approved Qatar pathway for recurrent nosebleeds or bleeding-risk factors. Call Back If: nosebleeds becoming more frequent or heavier.

careAdvice.titleEn: Home first aid for a nosebleed
careAdvice.instructionTextEn: Sit down, lean forward with the head tilted forward, pinch the soft part of the nose just above the nostrils for 10-15 minutes, and breathe through the mouth. An ice pack may help. Call Back If: bleeding continues past 10-15 minutes of pinching; feeling weak or dizzy.

Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care.

Is the skin blistered?
Has a temperature been measured? If so, what was it?

questions.questionTextEn: Is this an electrical or lightning injury, or is there confusion, fainting, a very high temperature with no sweating, or a rapid heartbeat suggesting heatstroke rather than simple sunburn?
questions.rationaleEn: Electrical and lightning injuries retain a conservative emergency disposition because their authored protocol is not in the generated catalog. NHS.UK also notes severe sunburn can progress to heat exhaustion and heatstroke, which needs emergency care.

questions.questionTextEn: Is the skin blistered or swollen, is the temperature very high or does the caller feel hot, cold, or shivery, does the caller feel very tired, dizzy, or sick, is there a headache or muscle cramps, or is the patient a baby or young child?

questions.questionTextEn: Is this mild-to-moderate sunburn without blistering or the features above?
questions.rationaleEn: NHS.UK guidance describes most sunburn as resolving within about a week with home care.

careAdvice.instructionTextEn: Call Qatar emergency services on 999 and do not drive for confusion, seizure, collapse, abnormal breathing, very hot skin, inability to drink, severe dehydration, or an unwell infant/child. Move to shade or air conditioning, remove excess clothing, and cool with water and airflow while following 999 instructions. Do not use ice directly or give oral fluids if drowsy, vomiting, seizing, or unsafe to swallow. Call Qatar 999 now, follow the call-taker's ambulance and emergency-transport instructions, and do not self-drive. Do not delay emergency care. Call Back If: worsening confusion or collapse; seizure or abnormal breathing; inability to drink or markedly reduced urine.
Cool the skin, stay hydrated, and arrange same-day medical review, especially for blistering or a young child. Call Back If: fever worsens; increasing dizziness.

Leave the sun, cool skin with a cool shower or damp cloth, wear loose clothing, and maintain usual fluids if not restricted. Use only a bland unperfumed moisturiser on intact skin and do not burst blisters or apply ice. Medicine requires age, weight, pregnancy, allergy, kidney/liver disease, dehydration, and current-medicine checks. Call Back If: large blisters, facial/eye involvement, fever, dizziness, vomiting, reduced urine, or feeling very unwell.

guidelineRedirects.promptTextEn: Is this a burn from direct heat, flame, hot liquid, or steam rather than sun exposure?
Was the injury caused by an acid or another chemical rather than sun exposure?
